statement: As summarized by a 2010 narrative review (Degenhardt et al., 2010), studies of people who use ecstasy have found that some meet criteria for dependence, but the share ranges from about 4 in 100 to 73 in 100 depending on who was asked, how, and over what period. In two US household surveys, 3.6 in 100 people who had used ecstasy in the past year (Wu et al.) and 3.8 in 100 of those who had started within the previous two years (Stone et al.) met criteria for hallucinogen dependence. In a German community study, 0.4 in 100 of all young adults met past-year criteria for ecstasy, hallucinogen or stimulant dependence, and 5.8 in 100 of people who had ever used ecstasy had ever met criteria (about 12 of 207 people, by our arithmetic from the table). In samples recruited differently, 19 in 100 of New York nightclub attendees and 22 in 100 of Taiwanese juvenile detainees who used ecstasy met past-year criteria, and 16 to 18 in 100 in convenience samples in Germany, the UK and Australia (195, 1,106 and 1,662 people) were counted as dependent or scored above a screening scale's cut-off. The highest figures, 43, 64 and 73 in 100 over a lifetime, came from three small samples: 52 adolescents and young adults in drug treatment and in the community who had used ecstasy at least 5 times, 185 people the review describes as regularly using ecstasy, and 59 rave attendees who had taken at least 250 tablets in their lifetime. The review says all the instruments were designed for other drugs, only one study used a clinician's assessment, assessment was mostly by self-report and lifetime recall, and most samples were recruited by convenience or snowball methods, so the figures cannot be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy; it adds that people often reported dependence symptoms despite relatively infrequent use and that it is unclear whether they understood the questions as intended, and that pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some dependence may be on another drug. Across studies, the symptoms most often reported included continued use despite problems, spending a lot of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal; in two studies the symptoms fell into a group about compulsive use and a group about escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended). In the one study that followed people (the German community study above), 93 in 100 of those who met criteria at the start no longer did just over three years later and 50 in 100 had stopped using ecstasy altogether; the review does not give the size of that group, which by our arithmetic was about 12 to 14 people. In Australia, fewer than 1 in 100 treatment episodes were for ecstasy. The review also describes animal studies in which MDMA is rewarding but may be less so than other illicit drugs, and notes a lack of case reports of severe withdrawal. It concludes that the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is thin in scope and design.
plain: Some people who use ecstasy meet the criteria for dependence, but studies disagree widely on how many. In two US national surveys, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently did. In club-goer, detention and volunteer samples, 16 to 22 in 100 did. In three small samples, including people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 tablets, 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. Most studies recruited volunteers and used questionnaires made for other drugs, so the figures may not fit everyone who uses ecstasy. The one study that followed people for over three years found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were; that group was small, about 12 to 14 people by our arithmetic. Tolerance (needing more for the same effect) was among the symptoms people reported most, and in two studies it went together with using more, or for longer, than meant. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug. This comes second-hand, from a 2010 review.
population: People who use ecstasy in studies summarized by a 2010 narrative review: US and German general-population surveys, New York nightclub attendees, Taiwanese juvenile detainees, and convenience samples in Australia, Germany, the UK and the US (26 to 1,662 people per study)
exposure: Use of ecstasy (pills sold as ecstasy, contents not tested), from a few lifetime occasions to hundreds of tablets
comparator: None in most studies; one study compared ecstasy with other hallucinogens; one followed people over time
outcome: Meeting criteria for dependence on questionnaires or interviews designed for other drugs (DSM-IV hallucinogen or amphetamine criteria, CIDI, the Severity of Dependence Scale and others), past year, past month or lifetime
magnitude: Share meeting criteria, as printed in Table 1: general population: 3.8% past year (Stone, N 1199, people who started within 2 years), 3.6% past year (Wu, N 652; text says 4%, another 11% with one or two symptoms), 5.8% lifetime among people who had ever used ecstasy (von Sydow, N 207; about 12 people, editors' arithmetic) with 0.4% of all young adults dependent in the past year; sentinel samples: 19% past year (Parsons, N 214), 22% past year (Yen and Hsu, N 200); self-selected or convenience samples: 18% past month (Bruno, N 1662, scale cut-off 4 or more), 17% (Winstock, N 1106, scale cut-off 5 or more, timeframe not specified in the table, lifetime in the text), 16% (Tossman, N 195, timeframe not specified), 17% lifetime (Yacoubian, N 154, probable dependence), 43% lifetime (Cottler, N 52), 64% lifetime (Topp, N 185), 73% lifetime (Thomasius, N 59, at least 250 lifetime tablets, clinician-rated); Hanson and Luciana (N 26): prevalence cell N = 2 but 14 met abuse or dependence criteria in the details column and text. Course (von Sydow, just over 3 years): 93% no longer dependent, 50% no longer using, 43% still using (group size not given; editors' arithmetic: about 12 to 14 people). Treatment: under 1% of Australian treatment episodes. No intervals are given.

evidence.locator: 2.1 Complicating issues in generalising laboratory research to recreational human use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review notes that pills sold as ecstasy may not contain MDMA at all, so people developing regular or dependent use of ecstasy may not be taking MDMA, and that some or many pills may contain methamphetamine, so people may develop dependence on methamphetamine rather than, or as well as, MDMA. Some studies controlled statistically for other drug use, including methamphetamine, but that use was self-reported, not confirmed by laboratory testing.

evidence.locator: Table 1, rows Stone et al. to Bruno et al. (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: Population-based samples: Stone et al. (US National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse, 2000-2001; N 1199; six items matching DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence criteria): 3.8% past year, among people who had started ecstasy within the previous two years. Von Sydow et al. (Germany, 1995-1999; representative sample aged 14-24; N 207; CIDI interview): 5.8% lifetime among people who had ever used ecstasy; less than 10% of those classed as lifetime dependent were past-year dependent at the 42-month follow-up. Wu et al. (US National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 2005; N 652; the same six hallucinogen items): 3.6% past year; another 11% reported one or two symptoms. Samples of sentinel populations: Parsons et al. (New York nightclub attendees aged 18-29 who had used ecstasy in the past 4 weeks; N 214; CIDI): 19% past year, with a median of 2.5 days of use in the past 4 months. Yen and Hsu (Taiwanese juvenile justice detainees who had used ecstasy; N 200): 22% past year. Self-selected sample: Bruno et al. (Australia, 2003-2004; N 1662; people using ecstasy at least monthly, recruited by purposive and snowball sampling; Severity of Dependence Scale score of 4 or more): 18% past month; among those screening positively, 49% used 1-2 times per week and 34% 1-2 times per month.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (continued), rows Cottler et al. to Thomasius et al. (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: Cottler et al. (US; adolescents and young adults in inpatient drug treatment and in the community, at least 5 lifetime occasions of use; N 52; computerised CIDI module): 43% lifetime; the most common symptoms were continued use despite problems (63%) and withdrawal (59%), and all dependent participants had tolerance or withdrawal. Hanson and Luciana (US students and community members; N 26; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): the prevalence cell reads N = 2 LT while the details column says 14 met the criteria. Scheier et al. (US and Australia; N 639; modified CIDI): no prevalence given, mean 227 lifetime pills. Topp et al. (Australia, 1997; N 185; CIDI): 64% lifetime; the authors questioned how withdrawal symptoms were endorsed. Tossman (Germany, 2002; N 195; people who used ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year): 16%, timeframe not specified. Yacoubian et al. (Washington rave attendees; N 154; a screening scale): 17% lifetime, 'probable' dependence. Thomasius et al. (Germany; rave attendees with at least 250 lifetime tablets, mean 794; N 59; clinical interview rated by clinical psychologists): 73% lifetime.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (continued), Winstock et al. row, and footnote; 3.2 Studies of ecstasy dependence among users, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6)
evidence.extracted: Winstock et al. (UK, 1999; readers of a dance music magazine who had ever used ecstasy; N 1106; Severity of Dependence Scale score of 5 or more): 17%, with a footnote that the timeframe was not specified; mean 160 lifetime occasions of use; tolerance and continued use despite problems with health, work or relationships were reported by more than half of the sample. Section 3.2: few studies have examined dependence among people who use ecstasy; all used instruments designed for other drugs, and just one (of a non-representative sample) involved clinician or psychiatric assessment. Topp et al. (1997): 64% of 185 people who regularly used ecstasy met lifetime criteria, typically during their heaviest use period, when 66% were using 1-2 times per week and 25% between 1 and 3 days per month; the authors questioned whether the withdrawal items separated comedown effects from dysphoria that eases with further use.

evidence.locator: 3.2, the paragraph beginning 'Two large survey samples of dependence' and the paragraph beginning 'Studies of dependence among ecstasy users in representative general population samples are limited'
evidence.extracted: Two large samples used the five-item Severity of Dependence Scale, which measures compulsion to use: in the UK survey of 1106 dance-magazine readers 17% screened positive for lifetime ecstasy dependence, and in the Australian interview-based study of 1662 people who regularly used ecstasy, 18% screened positive; of these 49% used ecstasy 1-2 times per week, 34% used 1-3 times per month and only 2% (n = 7) were using at least every second day, and financial, legal and work harms, sexual risk, overdose and help seeking were more common than among those who screened negative, independent of problematic methamphetamine use. In general population samples a German study found that past-year ecstasy/hallucinogen/stimulant dependence among all young adults was 0.4%; a US study found that 4% of people who had used ecstasy in the past year met DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence criteria (another 11% reported one or two symptoms) (Wu et al.), and 3.82% of those who had started ecstasy in the previous two years had developed dependence (Stone et al.); some have argued that grouping ecstasy with the hallucinogens in DSM-IV may not fit the behavioural data.

evidence.locator: 3.3 The structure of ecstasy dependence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (the 3rd begins on p. 7 and ends on p. 8)
evidence.extracted: Two studies of the structure of the symptoms, both in Australian samples (one also in US samples): Topp et al. (1997) found for ecstasy, unlike alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids, two separate components, compulsive use (use despite problems, giving up activities, unsuccessful attempts to stop, withdrawal, excessive time spent) and escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended); Bruno et al. (2009) found two related factors with the same names for the Severity of Dependence Scale. The review concludes that the dependence syndrome may not be of the same nature as for alcohol, opioids and amphetamine, and that behavioural reinforcement or learning may play a part for some people.

evidence.locator: 3.4 The course of ecstasy dependence; 3.5 Treatment seeking for ecstasy-related problems, 1st paragraph (p. 8)
evidence.extracted: Course: only one study has followed people who met DSM-IV criteria for ecstasy dependence (von Sydow et al., 2002; a German population-based study of young adults with a mean follow-up of just over three years): 93% were no longer dependent at follow-up; 50% were no longer using the drug at all, and of the 43% still using, the majority did not meet criteria for a use disorder; the authors suggested that ecstasy dependence might be a transient phenomenon. Treatment: routine data in Australia show very small numbers of treatment episodes for ecstasy (less than 1% of all episodes), consistent with surveys finding that treatment seeking is infrequent even among people who report concerns about their use.

evidence.locator: 3.6 Limitations of existing human evidence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; 4 Summary and implications, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 8)
evidence.extracted: Limitations: the studies are extremely heterogeneous in assessment methods and samples, which makes meta-analysis inappropriate; dependence was typically assessed by self-report without clinician verification, usually as lifetime retrospective reports; despite relatively infrequent use even at their heaviest, people very commonly reported dependence symptoms, and it is unclear whether participants understood the questions as the investigators intended; the prevalence cannot be extrapolated to all people who use ecstasy because most studies recruited people with recent use by convenience or snowball sampling; information on the natural history comes mostly from retrospective reports of convenience samples. Summary: the review judges the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome to be restricted in how much was studied and in how it was studied (see the quotation); animal evidence suggests MDMA may be a less potent reinforcer than other drugs but still has dependence potential; some people report problems controlling their use and concern about it, but there is a notable lack of case reports of severe withdrawal, which suggests physical symptoms play a more limited role than psychological ones; tolerance and withdrawal have been reported, mostly in questionnaires designed for other drugs; treatment presentations are uncommon compared with the prevalence of use but do occur.
evidence.quote: The evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is limited in both scope and design.

risk_of_bias.note: Mostly convenience and snowball samples, instruments designed for other drugs, self-report and lifetime recall; the review itself calls the evidence limited, and some figures differ between its table and text.

inconsistency.note: Shares range from 3.6 to 73 in 100; most of the spread follows who was sampled and the period asked about, which the claim reports as a range instead of one number.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through a narrative review; pills sold as ecstasy may not be MDMA; the criteria were built for other drugs.

imprecision.note: No intervals; the highest figures come from samples of 52 to 185 people, and the 93 in 100 remission figure from a group the review does not size (about 12 to 14 people by editors' arithmetic).

grade.reasoning: Descriptive prevalence from observational studies starts low (METHODS 6.3); each of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision takes a level, so the result is very low. That some people meet criteria is better supported than any one percentage. Status replicated in direction only: every study finds some people meeting criteria, while the size varies widely, as the claim states (METHODS 6.4). Stays at draft because it rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3, 12). The claim reports findings, makes no statement about risk for any one person and gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Degenhardt et al. (2010) as summarized; none of the primary studies was read and none has a reference record here. The most useful to obtain, in order: von Sydow et al. (2002, German community study: the review does not size the group behind the 93% remission; 5.8% of 207 is about 12 and the 93, 50 and 43% fit 14, so it is a handful of people), Bruno et al. (2009, Australian SDS study), Stone et al. (2006, 2007) and Wu et al. (2008, US household surveys), Winstock et al. (2001), Topp et al. (1997). The review's table and text differ in places (Wu 3.6% in the table and 4% in the text; Bruno 1-2 against 1-3 times a month; Hanson and Luciana N = 2 in the table and 14 of 26 in the text; Winstock lifetime in the text but timeframe not specified in the table; Tossman's sample described as people who used ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year); the claim uses ranges and says so. The same text names 'escalating use' (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended) as one component, which is relevant to the 'I barely felt it' rule; the editor may link this claim to the tolerance claims.
